please create a simple summary of this repo so that I can pass the context to claude to help with more prompting.

addedLines: - architect: Designs system architecture and module boundaries before coding (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob)
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - API usage, tool use, Anthropic SDK usage. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- explorer: Maps unfamiliar codebases and reports findings concisely (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob)

- feature-dev:code-architect: Designs feature architectures by analyzing existing codebase patterns and conventions, then providing comprehensive implementation blueprints with specific files to create/modify, component designs, data flows, and build sequences (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- feature-dev:code-explorer: Deeply analyzes existing codebase features by tracing execution paths, mapping architecture layers, understanding patterns and abstractions, and documenting dependencies to inform new development (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- feature-dev:code-reviewer: Reviews code for bugs, logic errors, security vulnerabilities, code quality issues, and adherence to project conventions, using confidence-based filtering to report only high-priority issues that truly matter (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-simplifier: Use this agent when code has been written or modified and needs to be simplified for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. This agent should be triggered automatically after completing a coding task or writing a logical chunk of code. It simplifies code by following project best practices while retaining all functionality. The agent focuses only on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise.

Examples:

<example>
Context: The assistant has just implemented a new feature that adds user authentication to an API endpoint.
user: "Please add authentication to the /api/users endpoint"
assistant: "I've implemented the authentication for the /api/users endpoint. Here's the code:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
Since a logical chunk of code has been written (authentication feature), use the Task tool to launch the code-simplifier agent to improve the code's clarity and maintainability while preserving functionality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now let me use the code-simplifier agent to refine this implementation for better clarity and maintainability"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just fixed a bug by adding several conditional checks.
user: "Fix the null pointer exception in the data processor"
assistant: "I've added the necessary null checks to prevent the exception:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After modifying code to fix a bug, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the fix follows best practices and maintains code quality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Let me refine this bug fix using the code-simplifier agent to ensure it follows our best practices"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just refactored a function to improve performance.
user: "Optimize the data sorting algorithm for better performance"
assistant: "I've optimized the sorting algorithm. Here's the updated implementation:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After completing a performance optimization task, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and maintainable.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now I'll use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and follows our coding standards"
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. This includes (1) after generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) when reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, and (4) when you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:pr-test-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to review a pull request for test coverage quality and completeness. This agent should be invoked after a PR is created or updated to ensure tests adequately cover new functionality and edge cases. Typical triggers include the user asking whether tests on a freshly-created PR are thorough, an updated PR adding new logic that needs coverage analysis, and a final pre-merge double-check before marking a PR ready. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter: Use this agent when reviewing code changes in a pull request to identify silent failures, inadequate error handling, and inappropriate fallback behavior. This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. Examples:

<example>
Context: Daisy has just finished implementing a new feature that fetches data from an API with fallback behavior.
Daisy: "I've added error handling to the API client. Can you review it?"
Assistant: "Let me use the silent-failure-hunter agent to thoroughly examine the error handling in your changes."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has created a PR with changes that include try-catch blocks.
Daisy: "Please review PR #1234"
Assistant: "I'll use the silent-failure-hunter agent to check for any silent failures or inadequate error handling in this PR."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has just refactored error handling code.
Daisy: "I've updated the error handling in the authentication module"
Assistant: "Let me proactively use the silent-failure-hunter agent to ensure the error handling changes don't introduce silent failures."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:type-design-analyzer: Use this agent when you need expert analysis of type design in your codebase. Specifically use it (1) when introducing a new type to ensure it follows best practices for encapsulation and invariant expression, (2) during pull request creation to review all types being added, and (3) when refactoring existing types to improve their design quality. The agent will provide both qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings on encapsulation, invariant expression, usefulness, and enforcement. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)
- reviewer: Reviews recent diffs for bugs, security issues, and style (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)
- tester: Writes and runs tests for new or modified code (Tools: Read, Write, Edit, Bash)

- explain: Walk me through existing code section by section

- plan-feature: Enter plan mode and produce a detailed plan for a feature

- claude-md-management:claude-md-improver: Audit and improve CLAUDE.md files in repositories. Use when user asks to check, audit, update, improve, or fix CLAUDE.md files. Scans for all CLAUDE.md files, evaluates quality against templates, outputs quality report, then makes targeted updates. Also use when the user mentions "CLAUDE.md maintenance" or "project memory optimization".
- skill-creator:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

1	# Silmulator
2	
3	**SIL/HIL/CIL Hardware Simulator** — A PyQt6 GUI application for debugging embedded software against simulated lab instruments that behave per their real device specifications.
4	
5	## Documentation
6	
7	| Guide | Description |
8	|---|---|
9	| [User Guide](docs/user_guide.md) | Installation, quick start, virtual hardware reference, troubleshooting |
10	| [Developer Guide](docs/developer_guide.md) | Architecture, device layer, GUI layer, adding devices |
11	| [Adding Blocks](docs/adding_blocks.md) | Step-by-step guide to creating new hardware blocks |
12	| [Architecture Diagrams](docs/architecture.md) | Mermaid diagrams: system overview, data flow, class hierarchy |
13	| [Docker Guide](docker/README.md) | Browser (NoVNC) and native window Docker usage |
14	| [C++ Core](cpp_core/README.md) | SCPI parser build, API reference, Doxygen instructions |
15	| [Python Package](silmulator/README.md) | Package structure, library API reference |
16	| [Word User Guide](docs/Silmulator_User_Guide.docx) | Official Microsoft Word version for distribution |
17	
18	## Overview
19	
20	Silmulator provides a drag-and-drop canvas where you place virtual hardware blocks — oscilloscopes, power supplies, function generators, multimeters, and MSP430 microcontrollers — connect them with virtual wires, and interact with them using real SCPI commands. A code-input block parses your C/C++/Python source and routes the SCPI calls to the connected devices.
21	
22	This lets you test and debug measurement code **without physical hardware**, catching command errors and response-handling bugs at your desk.
23	
24	## Architecture
25	
26	```
27	Silmulator/
28	├── main.py                        # CLI entry point
29	├── setup.py                       # pip install support
30	├── requirements.txt               # Python dependencies
31	├── CMakeLists.txt                 # C++ build root
32	│
33	├── cpp_core/                      # High-performance C++ SCPI parser
34	│   ├── CMakeLists.txt
35	│   ├── include/
36	│   │   ├── scpi_parser.h          # Parser class declaration
37	│   │   └── scpi_types.h           # ScpiCommand, ScpiToken, etc.
38	│   └── src/
39	│       ├── scpi_parser.cpp        # Parser implementation
40	│       └── bindings.cpp           # pybind11 Python bindings
41	│
42	└── silmulator/                    # Python package
43	    ├── app.py                     # Application entry point
44	    ├── scpi/
45	    │   └── parser.py              # Pure-Python SCPI parser (fallback)
46	    ├── devices/
47	    │   ├── base_device.py         # Abstract SCPI device base
48	    │   ├── oscilloscope.py        # Tektronix MSO54-compatible
49	    │   ├── power_supply.py        # Keysight E36312A-compatible
50	    │   ├── function_generator.py  # Keysight 33522B-compatible
51	    │   ├── multimeter.py          # Keysight 34401A-compatible
52	    │   └── msp430.py              # TI MSP430FR5994-compatible
53	    ├── gui/
54	    │   ├── main_window.py         # PyQt6 main window
55	    │   ├── canvas.py              # Drag-and-drop scene + view
56	    │   └── blocks/
57	    │       ├── base_block.py      # Abstract block base class
58	    │       ├── oscilloscope_block.py
59	    │       ├── power_supply_block.py
60	    │       ├── function_generator_block.py
61	    │       ├── multimeter_block.py
62	    │       ├── msp430_block.py
63	    │       └── code_input_block.py
64	    ├── code_parser/
65	    │   └── base_parser.py         # C/C++/Python SCPI extractor
66	    └── utils/
67	        ├── waveform.py            # Waveform generation (numpy)
68	        └── signals.py             # Qt signal bus
69	```
70	
71	## Simulated Instruments
72	
73	### Oscilloscope (Tektronix MSO54-compatible)
74	- 4 analog channels (CH1–CH4)
75	- Full `ACQ`, `CH`, `CURSOR`, `DATA`, `DISPLAY`, `HORIZONTAL`, `MEASUREMENT`, `SELECT`, `TRIGGER`, `WFMPRE` command trees
76	- Waveform generation and `CURVE?` data transfer (ASCII and binary encoding)
77	- Live waveform injection via `inject_waveform(source, array)`
78	- 8 configurable measurements: FREQUENCY, PERIOD, AMPLITUDE, RMS, MEAN, HIGH, LOW, PK2PK, RISE, FALL, PDUTY, NDUTY
79	
80	### Power Supply (Keysight E36312A-compatible)
81	- 3 independent channels
82	- `SOURCE:VOLTAGE`, `SOURCE:CURRENT`, `OUTPUT`, `MEASURE`, `TRIGGER`, `INSTRUMENT` command trees
83	- OVP/OCP protection simulation
84	- `APPLY` combined set command
85	- Channel-by-channel tracking mode
86	
87	### Function Generator (Keysight 33522B-compatible)
88	- 2 independent channels (SOURCE1, SOURCE2)
89	- Functions: SIN, SQU, RAMP, PULS, NOIS, DC, USER, ARB
90	- AM, FM, PM, PWM modulation
91	- Burst and sweep modes
92	- Arbitrary waveform catalog
93	
94	### Multimeter (Keysight 34401A-compatible)
95	- Functions: VOLT:DC, VOLT:AC, CURR:DC, CURR:AC, RES, FRES, FREQ, PER, CONT, DIOD, TEMP
96	- `CONFIGURE`, `MEASURE`, `READ`, `FETCH`, `INITIATE` modes
97	- `CALCULATE` (null, limits, dB, statistics)
98	- `TRIGGER` and `SAMPLE` subsystems
99	- `DATA` buffer with `INITIATE`/`FETCH` workflow
100	- Measurement injection via `inject(function, value)`
101	
102	### MSP430 (TI MSP430FR5994-compatible)
103	- 8 GPIO ports (P1–P8) with direction, pull-up/down, interrupt control
104	- 12-channel 12-bit ADC with voltage injection
105	- 3x Timer_A, 1x Timer_B with capture-compare
106	- 4x UART (eUSCI_A) with full serial config
107	- 2x SPI (eUSCI_B) with CPOL/CPHA and transfer simulation
108	- 4x I2C with address, frequency, master/slave modes
109	- Unified Clock System (DCO, LFXT, SMCLK, MCLK, ACLK)
110	- Power management modes (AM, LPM0–LPM4.5)
111	- 16-register CPU state, PC control, memory map read/write
112	
113	## SCPI Command Examples
114	
115	```python
116	from silmulator.devices import Oscilloscope, PowerSupply, FunctionGenerator
117	
118	# Oscilloscope
119	osc = Oscilloscope()
120	osc.process("CH1:SCALE 0.5")           # 500mV/div
121	osc.process("HOR:SCALE 1E-3")          # 1ms/div
122	osc.process("TRIG:A:EDGE:SOURCE CH1")
123	osc.process("TRIG:A:LEVEL 1.5")
124	osc.process("ACQ:STATE 1")             # Run
125	freq = osc.process("MEASUREMENT:MEAS1:TYPE FREQUENCY; VALUE?")
126	data = osc.process("CURVE?")           # Get waveform data
127	
128	# Power Supply
129	psu = PowerSupply()
130	psu.process("INST:NSEL 1")
131	psu.process("VOLT 3.3")
132	psu.process("CURR 1.0")
133	psu.process("OUTP ON")
134	voltage = psu.process("MEAS:VOLT:DC?")
135	
136	# Function Generator
137	fgen = FunctionGenerator()
138	fgen.process("SOURCE1:FUNC SIN")
139	fgen.process("SOURCE1:FREQ 1000")
140	fgen.process("SOURCE1:VOLT 2.0")
141	fgen.process("OUTPUT1 ON")
142	
143	# MSP430
144	mcu = MSP430()
145	mcu.process("GPIO:PORT1:DIRECTION 0xFF")  # All outputs
146	mcu.process("GPIO:PORT1:OUTPUT 0x01")     # P1.0 HIGH
147	mcu.process("ADC:CHANNEL0:INJECT 1.65")  # Inject 1.65V
148	raw = mcu.process("ADC:CONVERT 0")       # Read raw ADC value
149	```
150	
151	## C++ Core
152	
153	The C++ SCPI parser (`cpp_core/`) provides a high-performance parsing backend with pybind11 Python bindings. It is optional — the pure-Python `silmulator/scpi/parser.py` is used automatically when the C++ extension is not built.
154	
155	### Building the C++ extension
156	
157	```bash
158	mkdir build && cd build
159	cmake ..
160	make -j4
161	# Copy the resulting scpi_core.so to silmulator/scpi/
162	```
163	
164	## Code Parser
165	
166	The `CodeInputBlock` on the canvas parses C, C++, or Python source code to extract SCPI command strings:
167	
168	**Recognized C/C++ patterns:**
169	```c
170	viWrite(session, "VOLT 5.0");
171	viQueryf(session, "MEAS:VOLT:DC?", result);
172	visa_write(dev, "OUTP ON");
173	scpi_send(handle, "ACQ:STATE 1");
174	ibwrt(dev, "TRIG:A:LEVEL 1.5");
175	```
176	
177	**Recognized Python patterns:**
178	```python
179	inst.write("VOLT 5.0")
180	result = inst.query("MEAS:VOLT:DC?")
181	rm.open_resource("GPIB::1").write("OUTP ON")
182	```
183	
184	## GUI Usage
185	
186	1. **Launch:** `python main.py`
187	2. **Add blocks:** Double-click items in the Library panel, or click toolbar buttons
188	3. **Connect blocks:** Click a port circle on one block, drag to a port on another
189	4. **Send commands:** Select a block → right-click → "Send SCPI command", or use the SCPI Console at the bottom
190	5. **Paste code:** Add a "Code Input" block → double-click to open the editor → paste your C/C++/Python code → click "Parse" to extract SCPI commands
191	6. **Run commands:** After connecting a Code Input block to hardware blocks, right-click → "Run parsed commands"
192	7. **Save/Load layouts:** File → Save (`.sil` JSON format)
193	
194	### Keyboard shortcuts
195	
196	| Key | Action |
197	|-----|--------|
198	| `Delete` | Remove selected blocks |
199	| `Ctrl+A` | Select all |
200	| `Ctrl+N` | New canvas |
201	| `Ctrl+O` | Open layout |
202	| `Ctrl+S` | Save layout |
203	| `Ctrl+0` | Reset zoom |
204	| `Ctrl+Shift+F` | Fit all blocks in view |
205	| Middle mouse drag | Pan |
206	| Scroll wheel | Zoom in/out |
207	
208	## Running Tests
209	
210	```bash
211	# Install dependencies
212	pip install -r requirements.txt
213	
214	# Run all tests
215	python -m pytest tests/ -v
216	
217	# Run specific device tests
218	python -m pytest tests/test_oscilloscope.py -v
219	python -m pytest tests/test_power_supply.py -v
220	python -m pytest tests/test_function_generator.py -v
221	python -m pytest tests/test_multimeter.py -v
222	python -m pytest tests/test_msp430.py -v
223	python -m pytest tests/test_scpi_parser.py -v
224	```
225	
226	## Requirements
227	
228	- Python 3.9+
229	- PyQt6 >= 6.4.0
230	- numpy >= 1.24.0
231	- scipy >= 1.10.0
232	
233	Optional (for C++ parser):
234	- CMake >= 3.16
235	- pybind11 >= 2.10.0
236	- C++17 compiler (GCC, Clang, or MSVC)
237	
238	## Design Decisions
239	
240	**SCPI compliance:** Each device implements the command set from its respective programmer's reference manual. Short forms (e.g., `VOLT` for `VOLTAGE`, `MEAS` for `MEASURE`) are registered alongside long forms for compatibility with real test code.
241	
242	**Simulation fidelity:** Measurements return the configured/injected values plus a small Gaussian noise term (≈1e-5 relative), mimicking real instrument behavior. You can override this with `inject(function, value)` for deterministic testing.
243	
244	**Pure-Python fallback:** The SCPI parser has both a C++ and Python implementation. The Python version is always available; the C++ version improves throughput for high-rate command streaming.
245	
246	**State isolation:** Each device instance maintains fully independent state. Running `*RST` returns all parameters to their power-on defaults without affecting other devices.
247

| [User Guide](docs/user_guide.md) | Installation, quick start, virtual hardware reference, troubleshooting |
| [Developer Guide](docs/developer_guide.md) | Architecture, device layer, GUI layer, adding devices |
| [Adding Blocks](docs/adding_blocks.md) | Step-by-step guide to creating new hardware blocks |
| [Architecture Diagrams](docs/architecture.md) | Mermaid diagrams: system overview, data flow, class hierarchy |
| [Docker Guide](docker/README.md) | Browser (NoVNC) and native window Docker usage |
| [C++ Core](cpp_core/README.md) | SCPI parser build, API reference, Doxygen instructions |
| [Python Package](silmulator/README.md) | Package structure, library API reference |
| [Word User Guide](docs/Silmulator_User_Guide.docx) | Official Microsoft Word version for distribution |

## Overview

Silmulator provides a drag-and-drop canvas where you place virtual hardware blocks — oscilloscopes, power supplies, function generators, multimeters, and MSP430 microcontrollers — connect them with virtual wires, and interact with them using real SCPI commands. A code-input block parses your C/C++/Python source and routes the SCPI calls to the connected devices.

This lets you test and debug measurement code **without physical hardware**, catching command errors and response-handling bugs at your desk.

## Architecture

```
Silmulator/
├── main.py                        # CLI entry point
├── setup.py                       # pip install support
├── requirements.txt               # Python dependencies
├── CMakeLists.txt                 # C++ build root
│
├── cpp_core/                      # High-performance C++ SCPI parser
│   ├── CMakeLists.txt
│   ├── include/
│   │   ├── scpi_parser.h          # Parser class declaration
│   │   └── scpi_types.h           # ScpiCommand, ScpiToken, etc.
│   └── src/
│       ├── scpi_parser.cpp        # Parser implementation
│       └── bindings.cpp           # pybind11 Python bindings
│
└── silmulator/                    # Python package
    ├── app.py                     # Application entry point
    ├── scpi/
    │   └── parser.py              # Pure-Python SCPI parser (fallback)
    ├── devices/
    │   ├── base_device.py         # Abstract SCPI device base
    │   ├── oscilloscope.py        # Tektronix MSO54-compatible
    │   ├── power_supply.py        # Keysight E36312A-compatible
    │   ├── function_generator.py  # Keysight 33522B-compatible
    │   ├── multimeter.py          # Keysight 34401A-compatible
    │   └── msp430.py              # TI MSP430FR5994-compatible
    ├── gui/
    │   ├── main_window.py         # PyQt6 main window
    │   ├── canvas.py              # Drag-and-drop scene + view
    │   └── blocks/
    │       ├── base_block.py      # Abstract block base class
    │       ├── oscilloscope_block.py
    │       ├── power_supply_block.py
    │       ├── function_generator_block.py
    │       ├── multimeter_block.py
    │       ├── msp430_block.py
    │       └── code_input_block.py
    ├── code_parser/
    │   └── base_parser.py         # C/C++/Python SCPI extractor
    └── utils/
        ├── waveform.py            # Waveform generation (numpy)
        └── signals.py             # Qt signal bus
```

## Simulated Instruments

### Oscilloscope (Tektronix MSO54-compatible)
- 4 analog channels (CH1–CH4)
- Full `ACQ`, `CH`, `CURSOR`, `DATA`, `DISPLAY`, `HORIZONTAL`, `MEASUREMENT`, `SELECT`, `TRIGGER`, `WFMPRE` command trees
- Waveform generation and `CURVE?` data transfer (ASCII and binary encoding)
- Live waveform injection via `inject_waveform(source, array)`
- 8 configurable measurements: FREQUENCY, PERIOD, AMPLITUDE, RMS, MEAN, HIGH, LOW, PK2PK, RISE, FALL, PDUTY, NDUTY

### Power Supply (Keysight E36312A-compatible)
- 3 independent channels
- `SOURCE:VOLTAGE`, `SOURCE:CURRENT`, `OUTPUT`, `MEASURE`, `TRIGGER`, `INSTRUMENT` command trees
- OVP/OCP protection simulation
- `APPLY` combined set command
- Channel-by-channel tracking mode

### Function Generator (Keysight 33522B-compatible)
- 2 independent channels (SOURCE1, SOURCE2)
- Functions: SIN, SQU, RAMP, PULS, NOIS, DC, USER, ARB
- AM, FM, PM, PWM modulation
- Burst and sweep modes
- Arbitrary waveform catalog

### Multimeter (Keysight 34401A-compatible)
- Functions: VOLT:DC, VOLT:AC, CURR:DC, CURR:AC, RES, FRES, FREQ, PER, CONT, DIOD, TEMP
- `CONFIGURE`, `MEASURE`, `READ`, `FETCH`, `INITIATE` modes
- `CALCULATE` (null, limits, dB, statistics)
- `TRIGGER` and `SAMPLE` subsystems
- `DATA` buffer with `INITIATE`/`FETCH` workflow
- Measurement injection via `inject(function, value)`

### MSP430 (TI MSP430FR5994-compatible)
- 8 GPIO ports (P1–P8) with direction, pull-up/down, interrupt control
- 12-channel 12-bit ADC with voltage injection
- 3x Timer_A, 1x Timer_B with capture-compare
- 4x UART (eUSCI_A) with full serial config
- 2x SPI (eUSCI_B) with CPOL/CPHA and transfer simulation
- 4x I2C with address, frequency, master/slave modes
- Unified Clock System (DCO, LFXT, SMCLK, MCLK, ACLK)
- Power management modes (AM, LPM0–LPM4.5)
- 16-register CPU state, PC control, memory map read/write

## SCPI Command Examples

```python
from silmulator.devices import Oscilloscope, PowerSupply, FunctionGenerator

# Oscilloscope
osc = Oscilloscope()
osc.process("CH1:SCALE 0.5")           # 500mV/div
osc.process("HOR:SCALE 1E-3")          # 1ms/div
osc.process("TRIG:A:EDGE:SOURCE CH1")
osc.process("TRIG:A:LEVEL 1.5")
osc.process("ACQ:STATE 1")             # Run
freq = osc.process("MEASUREMENT:MEAS1:TYPE FREQUENCY; VALUE?")
data = osc.process("CURVE?")           # Get waveform data

# Power Supply
psu = PowerSupply()
psu.process("INST:NSEL 1")
psu.process("VOLT 3.3")
psu.process("CURR 1.0")
psu.process("OUTP ON")
voltage = psu.process("MEAS:VOLT:DC?")

# Function Generator
fgen = FunctionGenerator()
fgen.process("SOURCE1:FUNC SIN")
fgen.process("SOURCE1:FREQ 1000")
fgen.process("SOURCE1:VOLT 2.0")
fgen.process("OUTPUT1 ON")

# MSP430
mcu = MSP430()
mcu.process("GPIO:PORT1:DIRECTION 0xFF")  # All outputs
mcu.process("GPIO:PORT1:OUTPUT 0x01")     # P1.0 HIGH
mcu.process("ADC:CHANNEL0:INJECT 1.65")  # Inject 1.65V
raw = mcu.process("ADC:CONVERT 0")       # Read raw ADC value
```

## C++ Core

The C++ SCPI parser (`cpp_core/`) provides a high-performance parsing backend with pybind11 Python bindings. It is optional — the pure-Python `silmulator/scpi/parser.py` is used automatically when the C++ extension is not built.

### Building the C++ extension

```bash
mkdir build && cd build
cmake ..
make -j4
# Copy the resulting scpi_core.so to silmulator/scpi/
```

## Code Parser

The `CodeInputBlock` on the canvas parses C, C++, or Python source code to extract SCPI command strings:

**Recognized C/C++ patterns:**
```c
viWrite(session, "VOLT 5.0");
viQueryf(session, "MEAS:VOLT:DC?", result);
visa_write(dev, "OUTP ON");
scpi_send(handle, "ACQ:STATE 1");
ibwrt(dev, "TRIG:A:LEVEL 1.5");
```

**Recognized Python patterns:**
```python
inst.write("VOLT 5.0")
result = inst.query("MEAS:VOLT:DC?")
rm.open_resource("GPIB::1").write("OUTP ON")
```

## GUI Usage

1. **Launch:** `python main.py`
2. **Add blocks:** Double-click items in the Library panel, or click toolbar buttons
3. **Connect blocks:** Click a port circle on one block, drag to a port on another
4. **Send commands:** Select a block → right-click → "Send SCPI command", or use the SCPI Console at the bottom
5. **Paste code:** Add a "Code Input" block → double-click to open the editor → paste your C/C++/Python code → click "Parse" to extract SCPI commands
6. **Run commands:** After connecting a Code Input block to hardware blocks, right-click → "Run parsed commands"
7. **Save/Load layouts:** File → Save (`.sil` JSON format)

### Keyboard shortcuts

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| `Delete` | Remove selected blocks |
| `Ctrl+A` | Select all |
| `Ctrl+N` | New canvas |
| `Ctrl+O` | Open layout |
| `Ctrl+S` | Save layout |
| `Ctrl+0` | Reset zoom |
| `Ctrl+Shift+F` | Fit all blocks in view |
| Middle mouse drag | Pan |
| Scroll wheel | Zoom in/out |

## Running Tests

```bash
# Install dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt

# Run all tests
python -m pytest tests/ -v

# Run specific device tests
python -m pytest tests/test_oscilloscope.py -v
python -m pytest tests/test_power_supply.py -v
python -m pytest tests/test_function_generator.py -v
python -m pytest tests/test_multimeter.py -v
python -m pytest tests/test_msp430.py -v
python -m pytest tests/test_scpi_parser.py -v
```

## Requirements

- Python 3.9+
- PyQt6 >= 6.4.0
- numpy >= 1.24.0
- scipy >= 1.10.0

Optional (for C++ parser):
- CMake >= 3.16
- pybind11 >= 2.10.0
- C++17 compiler (GCC, Clang, or MSVC)

## Design Decisions

**SCPI compliance:** Each device implements the command set from its respective programmer's reference manual. Short forms (e.g., `VOLT` for `VOLTAGE`, `MEAS` for `MEASURE`) are registered alongside long forms for compatibility with real test code.

**Simulation fidelity:** Measurements return the configured/injected values plus a small Gaussian noise term (≈1e-5 relative), mimicking real instrument behavior. You can override this with `inject(function, value)` for deterministic testing.

**Pure-Python fallback:** The SCPI parser has both a C++ and Python implementation. The Python version is always available; the C++ version improves throughput for high-rate command streaming.

**State isolation:** Each device instance maintains fully independent state. Running `*RST` returns all parameters to their power-on defaults without affecting other devices.

Here's a paste-ready summary of the repo. Copy the block below into any Claude conversation as context:

```markdown
# Silmulator — Repo Summary

## What it is
Silmulator is a SIL/HIL/CIL hardware simulator: a PyQt6 desktop app for debugging
embedded/measurement software against simulated lab instruments that behave per
their real device specifications. Users drag virtual hardware blocks onto a canvas
(oscilloscope, power supply, function generator, multimeter, MSP430 MCU), wire
them together, and drive them with real SCPI commands — so measurement code can
be tested at a desk with no physical hardware. A "Code Input" block parses
C/C++/Python source (viWrite, inst.write/query, etc.), extracts the SCPI calls,
and routes them to the connected virtual devices.

## Tech stack
- Python 3.9+, PyQt6 (GUI), numpy/scipy (waveforms), pytest (tests)
- Optional C++17 SCPI parser (cpp_core/) with pybind11 bindings and CMake build;
  a pure-Python parser (silmulator/scpi/parser.py) is the always-available fallback
- Packaging: setup.py/pyproject.toml, uv.lock, PyInstaller spec, Docker
  (native window + browser NoVNC modes), NSIS Windows installer, macOS DMG

## Layout (main code lives in Silmulator/Silmulator/ inside the repo)
- main.py — CLI entry point; silmulator/app.py — application entry
- silmulator/devices/ — SCPI device simulations, one class per instrument:
  oscilloscope.py (Tektronix MSO54), power_supply.py (Keysight E36312A),
  function_generator.py (Keysight 33522B), multimeter.py (Keysight 34401A),
  msp430.py (TI MSP430FR5994: GPIO, ADC, timers, UART/SPI/I2C, clocks, LPM).
  All extend devices/base_device.py; each keeps independent state, supports
  *RST, SCPI short/long forms, small Gaussian measurement noise, and
  deterministic value injection (inject(...) / inject_waveform(...)).
- silmulator/gui/ — main_window.py, canvas.py (drag-drop scene, port-to-port
  wiring), blocks/ (one GUI block per device + code_input_block.py +
  custom_block.py), dialogs/device_config.py. Layouts save/load as .sil JSON.
- silmulator/scpi/parser.py — pure-Python SCPI parser (C++ scpi_core is optional)
- silmulator/code_parser/ — extracts SCPI strings from pasted C/C++/Python code
  (base_parser.py) and whole code projects (project.py)
- silmulator/custom_blocks/ — JSON block specs auto-loaded into the library at
  startup (also reads ~/.silmulator/custom_blocks/); a wizard can generate new
  blocks from vendor docs dropped in hardware_docs/
- silmulator/utils/ — waveform.py (numpy waveform generation), signals.py (Qt bus)
- tests/ — pytest suites per device plus SCPI parser, canvas connections,
  block creation, custom blocks, and code-project parsing
- docs/ — user guide, developer guide, adding_blocks.md, architecture diagrams
  (Mermaid), Doxyfile; repo root also has docs/learning/ (HTML lessons/drills)

## Key design decisions
- SCPI compliance per each instrument's programmer's reference manual
- C++ parser is a performance option, never a requirement (Python fallback)
- Device state isolation: instances are fully independent
- Run: `python main.py`; Test: `python -m pytest tests/ -v`
```

You are turning "the" into a structured, actionable plan document.

This command has two phases:
- PHASE 1: Interrogate the idea until it is unambiguous
- PHASE 2: Produce the plan document

Do not skip to Phase 2 until Phase 1 is complete.

---

## PHASE 1 — INTERROGATE THE IDEA

Read the codebase first so your questions are grounded in reality:
```bash
find src/ lib/ app/ -type f 2>/dev/null | head -30
git log --oneline -10
cat CLAUDE.md 2>/dev/null || true
```

Then ask clarifying questions — ONE at a time, wait for the answer,
then ask the next. Do not dump a list of questions all at once.
A question only gets asked if you genuinely cannot write a good plan
without knowing the answer.

Things worth asking about (pick the most important ones):

**Scope:**
- What does done look like? What can a user DO when this is complete?
- What is explicitly OUT of scope for this version?
- Is this a new feature, a change to existing behaviour, or a fix?

**Users and context:**
- Who uses this and in what situation?
- What do they have / know before they reach this feature?

**Technical constraints:**
- Does this touch existing code that other things depend on?
- Any performance, security, or compatibility requirements?
- Any third-party APIs or libraries involved?

**Edge cases:**
- What happens when the input is invalid or missing?
- What's the failure mode and how should it be handled?

**Priority:**
- Does this need to be done in a specific order relative to other work?
- Is there a simpler version that delivers most of the value?

Stop asking when you have enough to write a plan that could be handed
to a developer (or the overnight session) without them needing to ask
you anything.

---

## PHASE 2 — PRODUCE THE PLAN DOCUMENT

Save to `.claude/plans/[slug].md` where slug is a short dash-case
name derived from the idea. Example: "add weapon inventory" →
`.claude/plans/weapon-inventory.md`

The document structure:

```markdown
# Plan: [Feature Name]
Date: [date]
Status: READY FOR IMPLEMENTATION
Estimated complexity: S / M / L / XL

## The Idea (one paragraph)
[What this is, in plain language. Someone unfamiliar with the codebase
should understand this in 30 seconds.]

## Goal
[One sentence: what a user can DO when this is shipped that they
cannot do now.]

## Out of Scope (this version)
[Explicit list of things NOT included. This prevents scope creep
during implementation.]

## Affected Areas
[Files, modules, or systems this touches. Be specific.]
- `src/path/to/file.py` — [why it changes]
- `src/path/to/other.cpp` — [why it changes]
- New files needed: [list]

## Implementation Order
[Ordered steps. Each step should be independently committable.]

1. [Step 1 — what it produces]
2. [Step 2 — builds on step 1]
3. [Step 3 — etc.]

## Acceptance Criteria
[Testable conditions that define "done". Each one should be
verifiable by running a test or observing a specific behaviour.]

- [ ] [Given X, when Y, then Z]
- [ ] [Given X, when Y, then Z]
- [ ] Tests pass: [specific test file or command]

## Edge Cases and Error Handling
[What can go wrong and how each case is handled.]

| Situation | Expected behaviour |
|-----------|-------------------|
| [case] | [what happens] |

## Open Questions
[Anything still unresolved that will need a decision during implementation.
If there are none, write "None — plan is complete."]

## Suggested GitHub Issues
[If this plan should become overnight issues, list them here as a
starting point for /plan-github:]

1. [Issue title] — [one line scope]
2. [Issue title] — [one line scope]
3. [Issue title] — [one line scope]
```

---

## AFTER SAVING THE PLAN

Tell the user:
1. Where the plan was saved
2. How to turn it into GitHub issues:
   `/plan-github "[feature name]"` — or offer to run it now
3. How to start implementation immediately:
   `/develop [feature name]` — uses the plan as the spec
4. How to queue it for overnight:
   Add the suggested issues to GitHub, label ready-for-ai,
   then `bash ~/scripts/nightly.sh`

---

## TONE

Ask questions like a sharp senior engineer reviewing a spec —
direct, specific, not adversarial. The goal is to surface
assumptions before they become bugs, not to gatekeep.

If the idea is already clear enough to plan without questions,
say so briefly and go straight to the plan.

1	# Plan: MSP430 Realistic Fault & Drift Modeling
2	Date: 2026-07-05
3	Status: READY FOR IMPLEMENTATION
4	Estimated complexity: M
5	
6	## The Idea (one paragraph)
7	Extend `msp430.py` beyond clean Gaussian noise to model specific, datasheet-derived
8	imperfections: ADC12_B quantization/linearity error, DCO clock drift within its
9	tolerance band, and timer/capture jitter. The goal is a device that can teach a
10	user what a marginal or out-of-spec board looks like in software, not just a
11	perfect one — grounded in real tolerance numbers from TI's datasheet, not
12	invented values.
13	
14	## Goal
15	A user can enable a "corner-case" mode on the simulated MSP430 and see ADC
16	readings, timer captures, and clock-derived timing shift in ways that match the
17	datasheet's stated tolerance ranges — useful for testing whether their
18	measurement code has adequate error margins.
19	
20	## Out of Scope (this version)
21	- Modeling faults for the other four devices — MSP430 only
22	- Simulating catastrophic/destructive faults (pin shorts, overvoltage damage) —
23	  this pass is tolerance-band drift only, not failure injection
24	- A GUI control panel for fault parameters — device-model layer only this pass;
25	  GUI exposure is a follow-up
26	
27	## Affected Areas
28	- `silmulator/devices/msp430.py` — add drift/quantization model
29	- `silmulator/utils/waveform.py` — may need noise-shaping helpers beyond current Gaussian model
30	- New file: `tests/test_msp430_fault_modeling.py`
31	
32	## Implementation Order
33	1. Pull DCO frequency tolerance, ADC12_B INL/DNL and quantization step size, and timer jitter specs from the MSP430FR5994 datasheet (the datasheet has the numeric tolerances; the User's Guide doesn't)
34	2. Implement ADC quantization + INL/DNL as a deterministic function of the ideal reading, not just random noise
35	3. Implement DCO drift as a small frequency offset applied to all clock-derived timing (timers, UART actual-vs-nominal baud)
36	4. Add a device-level toggle: `nominal` vs `corner-case` (worst-case-within-spec) profiles
37	5. Validate against `inject()`/`inject_waveform()` — fault modeling should compose with existing deterministic injection, not replace it
38	
39	## Acceptance Criteria
40	- [ ] Given `corner-case` mode, ADC readings show quantization error consistent with the datasheet's stated LSB size
41	- [ ] Given `corner-case` mode, timer-derived durations shift by an amount within (not exceeding) the datasheet's DCO tolerance
42	- [ ] `nominal` mode behavior is unchanged from current `msp430.py` (no regression)
43	- [ ] Tests pass: `python -m pytest tests/test_msp430_fault_modeling.py -v`
44	
45	## Edge Cases and Error Handling
46	| Situation | Expected behaviour |
47	|-----------|-------------------|
48	| User calls `inject()` while `corner-case` mode is active | Injected value takes precedence; decide during implementation whether fault model layers on top |
49	| Datasheet gives a range rather than a single tolerance number | Sample within the range per-instance at `*RST`/construction, not per-read (part-to-part variation, not sample noise) |
50	
51	## Open Questions
52	- Should `corner-case` mode be one global switch, or per-peripheral (e.g. drifted clock but nominal ADC)? Leaning per-peripheral for teaching value — confirm.
53	
54	## Suggested GitHub Issues
55	1. `msp430: datasheet-grounded ADC12_B quantization/INL model`
56	2. `msp430: DCO drift model applied to timer-derived timing`
57	3. `msp430: nominal/corner-case profile toggle + injection composition rules`
58

perfect one — grounded in real tolerance numbers from TI's datasheet, not
invented values.

## Goal
A user can enable a "corner-case" mode on the simulated MSP430 and see ADC
readings, timer captures, and clock-derived timing shift in ways that match the
datasheet's stated tolerance ranges — useful for testing whether their
measurement code has adequate error margins.

## Out of Scope (this version)
- Modeling faults for the other four devices — MSP430 only
- Simulating catastrophic/destructive faults (pin shorts, overvoltage damage) —
  this pass is tolerance-band drift only, not failure injection
- A GUI control panel for fault parameters — device-model layer only this pass;
  GUI exposure is a follow-up

## Affected Areas
- `silmulator/devices/msp430.py` — add drift/quantization model
- `silmulator/utils/waveform.py` — may need noise-shaping helpers beyond current Gaussian model
- New file: `tests/test_msp430_fault_modeling.py`

## Implementation Order
1. Pull DCO frequency tolerance, ADC12_B INL/DNL and quantization step size, and timer jitter specs from the MSP430FR5994 datasheet (the datasheet has the numeric tolerances; the User's Guide doesn't)
2. Implement ADC quantization + INL/DNL as a deterministic function of the ideal reading, not just random noise
3. Implement DCO drift as a small frequency offset applied to all clock-derived timing (timers, UART actual-vs-nominal baud)
4. Add a device-level toggle: `nominal` vs `corner-case` (worst-case-within-spec) profiles
5. Validate against `inject()`/`inject_waveform()` — fault modeling should compose with existing deterministic injection, not replace it

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Given `corner-case` mode, ADC readings show quantization error consistent with the datasheet's stated LSB size
- [ ] Given `corner-case` mode, timer-derived durations shift by an amount within (not exceeding) the datasheet's DCO tolerance
- [ ] `nominal` mode behavior is unchanged from current `msp430.py` (no regression)
- [ ] Tests pass: `python -m pytest tests/test_msp430_fault_modeling.py -v`

## Edge Cases and Error Handling
| Situation | Expected behaviour |
|-----------|-------------------|
| User calls `inject()` while `corner-case` mode is active | Injected value takes precedence; decide during implementation whether fault model layers on top |
| Datasheet gives a range rather than a single tolerance number | Sample within the range per-instance at `*RST`/construction, not per-read (part-to-part variation, not sample noise) |

## Open Questions
- Should `corner-case` mode be one global switch, or per-peripheral (e.g. drifted clock but nominal ADC)? Leaning per-peripheral for teaching value — confirm.

## Suggested GitHub Issues
1. `msp430: datasheet-grounded ADC12_B quantization/INL model`
2. `msp430: DCO drift model applied to timer-derived timing`
3. `msp430: nominal/corner-case profile toggle + injection composition rules`

# Plan: MSP430 Spec-Driven Test Suite Expansion
Date: 2026-07-05
Status: READY FOR IMPLEMENTATION
Estimated complexity: S

## The Idea (one paragraph)
Generate a pytest suite for `msp430.py` that specifically covers the User's
Guide's stated edge cases and boundary conditions — invalid GPIO pin/mode
combinations, ADC reference-voltage boundaries, Timer_A capture/compare edge
conditions — rather than just extending happy-path coverage. Follow the
existing per-device test pattern already used for the other four instruments.

## Goal
`tests/` gains an MSP430 edge-case suite that would have caught the gaps found
by the compliance-auditor plan, so future changes to `msp430.py` can't silently
regress on spec compliance.

## Out of Scope (this version)
- Generating tests for the other four devices — MSP430 only
- Property-based/fuzz testing — this pass is doc-derived edge cases, explicit and enumerable
- Rewriting existing MSP430 tests — additive only

## Affected Areas
- `tests/` — existing per-device test pattern to follow
- `silmulator/devices/msp430.py` — target under test, read-only
- New file: `tests/test_msp430_edge_cases.py`

## Implementation Order
1. Pull boundary conditions from the User's Guide for the same pilot subsystems as the other MSP430 plans (ADC12_B, Timer_A, GPIO) — reuse that grounding rather than re-deriving it
2. Follow an existing device's test file structure/fixtures for consistency
3. Write one test per boundary condition, each with a comment citing the doc section it verifies
4. Run against current `msp430.py` — expect some failures; they should line up with the compliance audit's findings
5. Do not silently "fix" `msp430.py` to make tests pass — file failures as issues instead

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Every new test cites its source doc section in a comment
- [ ] Suite covers at minimum: invalid GPIO mode, ADC reference out-of-range, Timer_A capture/compare boundary
- [ ] Test failures against current code are captured as a list, not silently patched
- [ ] Tests pass: `python -m pytest tests/test_msp430_edge_cases.py -v` (post-fix, not necessarily on first run)

## Edge Cases and Error Handling
| Situation | Expected behaviour |
|-----------|-------------------|
| A boundary condition the doc describes has no corresponding command in `msp430.py` at all | Write the test as `xfail` with a comment explaining the dependency, not a silent skip |

## Open Questions

1. `tests: MSP430 GPIO invalid-mode edge cases`
2. `tests: MSP430 ADC12_B reference-voltage boundary cases`
3. `tests: MSP430 Timer_A capture/compare boundary cases`

# Plan: Implement All simulator_plans.zip Plans (MSP430 Quality Suite)
Date: 2026-07-05
Status: READY FOR IMPLEMENTATION
Estimated complexity: XL (umbrella over 5 plans: M + S + M + M + XL)

## The Idea (one paragraph)
`simulator_plans.zip` contains five READY plans that together form an MSP430
quality suite for Silmulator: audit the simulated MSP430 against real TI
documentation, add doc-derived edge-case tests, model realistic drift/faults,
semantically review pasted user code for sequencing bugs, and validate a
vendor-doc→block-spec generator against the hand-built device model. This
umbrella plan sequences all five, resolves their open questions, and corrects
two false assumptions found during grounding.

## Goal
A user gets a doc-cited compliance report for `msp430.py`, an edge-case test
suite guarding it, a datasheet-grounded corner-case simulation mode, sequencing
warnings in the Code Input block, and a doc→spec generator with a diff report —
all grounded in the actual SLAU367 User's Guide and MSP430FR5994 datasheet.

## Corrections to the source plans (found during grounding)
1. **TI docs are absent.** `hardware_docs/ti/` holds only `.gitkeep`. Decision:
   download SLAU367 + the MSP430FR5994 datasheet from ti.com into
   `hardware_docs/ti/MSP430FR5994/` before any doc-dependent step.
2. **The custom-block wizard does not exist.** Plan 2 assumes it does; only the
   JSON spec loader stub (`silmulator/custom_blocks/`) and `hello_world.json`
   exist. Decision (user-confirmed): build plan 2 from scratch as XL —
   doc→spec extraction pipeline plus diff comparator.

## Decisions adopted from the plans' open questions
- Audit: UNDOCUMENTED commands sit **outside** the compliance score.
- Generator: CONFLICT items **warn**, never block generation; report header
  records the SLAU367 revision used (whatever revision we download becomes the
  declared ground truth, since msp430.py's original source revision is unknown).
- Fault modeling: **per-peripheral** corner-case toggles (drifted clock with
  nominal ADC is a valid teaching configuration).
- Semantic reviewer: **flat** flagged/not-flagged list for v1 (plus the
  LOW_CONFIDENCE marker for ambiguous ordering, per that plan's edge cases).
- Test suite: runs **after** the audit so it targets the boundaries the audit
  proves matter.

## Out of Scope (this version)
- Everything the five plans individually exclude (other devices, GUI fault
  panel, auto-fixing user code, full peripheral coverage in the generator,
  auto-replacing msp430.py).
- Git/GitHub workflow — repo is not a git repository; work lands directly in
  the working tree this session.
- Fixing gaps the audit finds in `msp430.py` (its own follow-up plan), except
  where the edge-case test plan explicitly records failures as a list.

## Affected Areas
All paths relative to `Silmulator/Silmulator/`:
- `hardware_docs/ti/MSP430FR5994/` — downloaded SLAU367 + datasheet (new)
- `silmulator/devices/msp430.py` — read-only for plans 1/2/5; extended by plan 3
- `silmulator/utils/waveform.py` — possible noise-shaping helpers (plan 3)
- `silmulator/code_parser/base_parser.py`, `project.py` — semantic-review hook (plan 4)
- `silmulator/code_parser/semantic_review.py` — new (plan 4)
- `silmulator/gui/blocks/code_input_block.py` — surface findings (plan 4)
- `silmulator/custom_blocks/` — extraction pipeline + `diff_report.py` (plan 2)
- `scripts/audit_msp430.py`, `docs/audits/msp430-compliance-report.md` — new (plan 1)
- `tests/test_msp430_edge_cases.py`, `tests/test_msp430_fault_modeling.py`,
  `tests/test_semantic_review_msp430.py`, `tests/test_vendor_doc_diff.py` — new

## Implementation Order
1. **Docs**: download SLAU367 + MSP430FR5994 datasheet into `hardware_docs/ti/`
2. **Plan 1 — compliance auditor**: enumerate msp430.py SCPI surface, score
   against SLAU367 (ADC12_B + Timer_A at 100% coverage), emit re-runnable
   report via `scripts/audit_msp430.py`
3. **Plan 5 — edge-case tests**: doc-cited boundary tests for GPIO/ADC/Timer_A;
   failures recorded, not silently patched
4. **Plan 3 — fault/drift modeling**: datasheet-grounded ADC quantization/INL,

63	    """

73	        self._error_queue: List[tuple[int, str]] = []
74	        self._event_status_register: int = 0
75	        self._event_status_enable: int = 0
76	        self._service_request_enable: int = 0
77	        self._operation_complete: bool = False

88	        responses: List[str] = []

154	        self.reset()
155	        return ""

158	        self._error_queue.clear()

160	        return ""

"""Base class for all simulated SCPI instruments."""

from __future__ import annotations
from typing import Dict, Callable, Optional, List
from silmulator.scpi.parser import ScpiParser, ScpiCommand
import logging

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


class ScpiError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, code: int, msg: str):
        self.code = code
        self.msg = msg
        super().__init__(f"SCPI Error {code}: {msg}")


ERROR_MSGS = {
    -100: "Command error",
    -101: "Invalid character",
    -102: "Syntax error",
    -103: "Invalid separator",
    -104: "Data type error",
    -108: "Parameter not allowed",
    -109: "Missing parameter",
    -113: "Undefined header",
    -120: "Numeric data error",
    -121: "Invalid character in number",
    -123: "Exponent too large",
    -124: "Too many digits",
    -128: "Numeric data not allowed",
    -131: "Invalid suffix",
    -138: "Suffix not allowed",
    -148: "Character data not allowed",
    -150: "String data error",
    -151: "Invalid string data",
    -158: "String data not allowed",
    -160: "Block data error",
    -168: "Block data not allowed",
    -170: "Expression error",
    -178: "Expression data not allowed",
    -200: "Execution error",
    -220: "Parameter error",
    -221: "Settings conflict",
    -222: "Data out of range",
    -223: "Too much data",
    -224: "Illegal parameter value",
    -241: "Hardware missing",
    -310: "System error",
    -350: "Queue overflow",
    -410: "Query interrupted",
    -420: "Query unterminated",
    -430: "Query deadlocked",
    -440: "Query UNTERMINATED after indefinite response",
}


class BaseDevice:
    """Abstract base for all simulated SCPI instruments.

    Subclasses register handlers via `_register(path, fn)`.
    `process(cmd_string)` dispatches to the right handler.
    """

    MANUFACTURER = "Silmulator"
    MODEL = "BASE"
    SERIAL = "SIM000001"
    FIRMWARE = "1.0.0"

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._parser = ScpiParser()
        self._handlers: Dict[str, Callable[[ScpiCommand], str]] = {}
        self._error_queue: List[tuple[int, str]] = []
        self._event_status_register: int = 0
        self._event_status_enable: int = 0
        self._service_request_enable: int = 0
        self._operation_complete: bool = False
        self._output_queue: List[str] = []
        self._setup_common_handlers()
        self._setup_handlers()

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Public interface
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------

    def process(self, raw: str) -> str:
        """Process one or more SCPI commands and return response string."""
        responses: List[str] = []
        try:
            commands = self._parser.parse(raw.strip())
        except Exception as e:
            self._push_error(-100, str(e))
            return ""

        for cmd in commands:
            try:
                resp = self._dispatch(cmd)
                if resp is not None and resp != "":
                    responses.append(resp)
            except ScpiError as e:
                self._push_error(e.code, e.msg)
            except Exception as e:
                logger.exception("Unhandled error processing %s", cmd)
                self._push_error(-200, str(e))

        return "\n".join(responses)

    def reset(self) -> None:
        """Reset device to factory defaults."""
        self._error_queue.clear()
        self._event_status_register = 0
        self._event_status_enable = 0
        self._service_request_enable = 0
        self._operation_complete = False
        self._do_reset()

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Registration helpers
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------

    def _register(self, path: str, fn: Callable[[ScpiCommand], str]) -> None:
        self._handlers[path.upper()] = fn

    def _register_alias(self, alias: str, target: str) -> None:
        target_upper = target.upper()
        def handler(cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
            return self._handlers[target_upper](cmd)
        self._handlers[alias.upper()] = handler

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Common IEEE 488.2 handlers
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------

    def _setup_common_handlers(self) -> None:
        self._register("*IDN", self._idn)
        self._register("*RST", self._rst)
        self._register("*CLS", self._cls)
        self._register("*ESE", self._ese)
        self._register("*ESR", self._esr)
        self._register("*OPC", self._opc)
        self._register("*SRE", self._sre)
        self._register("*STB", self._stb)
        self._register("*TST", self._tst)
        self._register("*WAI", self._wai)
        self._register("SYSTEM:ERROR", self._sys_error)
        self._register("SYSTEM:ERROR:NEXT", self._sys_error)
        self._register("SYSTEM:ERROR:COUNT", self._sys_error_count)
        self._register("SYSTEM:VERSION", self._sys_version)

    def _idn(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
        return f"{self.MANUFACTURER},{self.MODEL},{self.SERIAL},{self.FIRMWARE}"

    def _rst(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
        self.reset()
        return ""

    def _cls(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
        self._error_queue.clear()
        self._event_status_register = 0
        return ""

    def _ese(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
        if cmd.is_query:
            return str(self._event_status_enable)
        if cmd.params:
            self._event_status_enable = int(float(cmd.params[0]))
        return ""

    def _esr(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
        val = self._event_status_register
        self._event_status_register = 0
        return str(val)

    def _opc(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
        if cmd.is_query:
            return "1"
        self._operation_complete = True
        self._event_status_register |= 1
        return ""

    def _sre(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
        if cmd.is_query:
            return str(self._service_request_enable)
        if cmd.params:
            self._service_request_enable = int(float(cmd.params[0]))
        return ""

    def _stb(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
        stb = 0
        if self._error_queue:
            stb |= 4
        if self._event_status_register & self._event_status_enable:
            stb |= 32
        if stb & self._service_request_enable:
            stb |= 64
        return str(stb)

    def _tst(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
        return "0"  # Self-test passed

    def _wai(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
        return ""

    def _sys_error(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
        if self._error_queue:
            code, msg = self._error_queue.pop(0)
            return f'{code},"{msg}"'
        return '0,"No error"'

    def _sys_error_count(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
        return str(len(self._error_queue))

    def _sys_version(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
        return "1999.0"

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Dispatch
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------

    def _dispatch(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
        path = cmd.path.upper()
        handler = self._handlers.get(path)
        if handler is None:
            # Try partial match for compound paths
            raise ScpiError(-113, f"Undefined header: {path}")
        return handler(cmd)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Error management
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------

    def _push_error(self, code: int, msg: Optional[str] = None) -> None:
        if msg is None:
            msg = ERROR_MSGS.get(code, "Unknown error")
        if len(self._error_queue) < 20:
            self._error_queue.append((code, msg))
        else:
            self._error_queue[-1] = (-350, "Queue overflow")

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Subclass hooks
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------

    def _setup_handlers(self) -> None:
        """Subclasses override to register device-specific handlers."""

    def _do_reset(self) -> None:
        """Subclasses override to reset device-specific state."""

289	        return ""

294	        return f"0x{effective & 0xFF:02X}"

297	        if cmd.params:

299	            p.output ^= mask

303	        if cmd.params:

305	            p.output |= mask

314	    def _gpio_pin_dir(self, cmd: ScpiCommand, p: GPIOPort) -> str:
315	        if not cmd.params:
316	            raise ScpiError(-109, "Missing parameter: pin number")
317	        pin = int(cmd.params[0])
318	        if len(cmd.params) < 2:
319	            return "OUTPUT" if p.direction & (1 << pin) else "INPUT"
320	        val = cmd.params[1].upper()
321	        if val in ("OUTPUT", "1", "OUT"):
322	            p.direction |= (1 << pin)
323	        elif val in ("INPUT", "0", "IN"):
324	            p.direction &= ~(1 << pin)
325	        return ""

327	    def _gpio_pin_val(self, cmd: ScpiCommand, p: GPIOPort) -> str:
328	        if not cmd.params:
329	            raise ScpiError(-109, "Missing parameter: pin number")
330	        pin = int(cmd.params[0])
331	        if len(cmd.params) < 2:
332	            if p.direction & (1 << pin):
333	                return "1" if p.output & (1 << pin) else "0"
334	            else:
335	                return "1" if p.input & (1 << pin) else "0"
336	        val = int(cmd.params[1])
337	        if val:
338	            p.output |= (1 << pin)
339	        else:
340	            p.output &= ~(1 << pin)
341	        return ""

833	    def _cpu_reg(self, cmd: ScpiCommand) -> str:
834	        if not cmd.params:
835	            raise ScpiError(-109, "Missing register number")
836	        reg = int(cmd.params[0])
837	        if not 0 <= reg <= 15:
838	            raise ScpiError(-222, "Register number out of range (0-15)")
839	        if cmd.is_query or len(cmd.params) < 2:
840	            return f"0x{self._registers[reg]:04X}"
841	        self._registers[reg] = int(cmd.params[1], 0) & 0xFFFF

programmable and selectable voltage levels (VR+ and VR-) to define the upper and lower limits of the
conversion. The digital output (NADC) is full scale (0FFFh) when the input signal is equal to or higher than
VR+, and is zero when the input signal is equal to or lower than VR-. The input channel and the reference
voltage levels (VR+ and VR-) are defined in the conversion-control memory.
